label: In-school practice
disclaimer: These are in-school practice items to review methods from class. They do not use real exam papers or high-score exemplars.

items.title: What lessons emphasise when organising a portfolio
items.question: When Form 6 opening lessons talk about checking and organising a portfolio, what do they emphasise?
options: Putting school admin steps into the lesson content
Using a clear structure to check and organise the work
Waiting for the year exam timetable before starting
Copying a real exam paper to fill the pages
items.explain: Lessons teach a method for checking and organising. They leave out school admin steps and year calendars.

items.title: Which two names appear in the Ming–Qing introduction
items.question: Which two painters does the Ming–Qing introduction first ask you to meet as a classroom starting point?
options: Only a list of names from an official exam paper
Any two names, with no need to look at the work
Shen Zhou and Wen Zhengming
No painters yet — only a ready-made name list
items.explain: The introduction meets Shen Zhou and Wen Zhengming, and sets them in dialogue with related contemporary approaches. It is not a course in copying famous paintings.

items.title: What to notice in the Bada Shanren lesson
items.question: In the Bada Shanren lesson, what does classroom looking emphasise?
options: Memorising comments from a real exam paper
Only counting how many birds were painted
Replacing your own looking with a high-score exemplar
How signs and identity can be presented
items.explain: The lesson looks at signs and the presentation of identity, not at memorising exam comments.

items.title: What the literati-painting introduction includes
items.question: Besides looking at traditional signs, what else does the literati-painting introduction include in class?
options: Copying a long question from a real exam paper
The Four Monks and related schools, plus practice describing brush, ink and possible meanings
Waiting for a ready-made prompt before starting
Only memorising school names, with no looking at form
items.explain: The introduction includes the Four Monks and related schools, and practises describing form, brush and ink, and possible meanings in class.

items.title: What to learn when comparing role-play methods
items.question: If the role-taking unit compares methods used by artists such as Cindy Sherman, what should you learn in class?
options: Copying a prompt from a real exam paper
Copying another artist’s work in full
How role-play can be used to discuss identity (method only)
Predicting whether you will get a high official mark
items.explain: The comparison is about method only. It does not copy an exam prompt or an artwork.

items.title: What to write in the Form 6 review
items.question: When reviewing a Form 6 portfolio, what is sound to write?
options: The wording of a high-score exemplar
A prediction of an official public-exam result
Only that everything has already been handed in
Strengths, next steps, and a short overview
items.explain: The review names strengths, next steps and an overview. It does not use real exam papers or high-score exemplars.

items.title: Ming–Qing looking and a contemporary method
items.question: Choose one Ming–Qing class observation and one related contemporary approach. Write what you learned about method: where comparison helps, and where you should not copy the picture. Do not copy a real exam paper.
items.hint: You may mention Shen Zhou, Wen Zhengming, the Young British Artists (YBA) or another class example, but stay with method.

items.title: Write how you would check that a portfolio is complete
items.question: Write how you would check whether a portfolio is complete: whether research notes, experiments, finished work and reflection are each visible. This is a checking method only — not a school admin step, and not a formal submission.
items.hint: A checklist style is enough, for example “research pages present / not yet present”. Do not write year calendars or admin steps.

items.title: Form 6 theme motive
items.question: In two sentences, write your Form 6 theme motive now. If the theme has already grown for a year, say what still holds and what you want to make more precise.
items.hint: Axis: theme clarity. Making it more precise does not mean inventing a brand-new slogan.

items.title: Form 6 material and comparison
items.question: Note one literati, Ming–Qing or related contemporary comparison, and one source you have followed up yourself. In one sentence each, say how it helps you now.
items.hint: Axis: research depth. Write the turn into your own work, not only a list of names.

items.title: Wet and dry media experiment
items.question: Describe one wet-or-dry or other Form 6 experiment: what you tried, what still needs adjusting, and how it serves the current piece.
items.hint: Axis: media and technique experiments. Keeping a trial page is more useful than keeping only the finished piece.

items.title: Portfolio organisation record
items.question: In three points, write what you noticed in your latest portfolio tidy: which kinds of pages are complete, which are still scattered, and which stack you will organise next.
items.hint: Axis: completeness of process record. This is an organising method, not an admin procedure.

items.title: What two pieces have taught you
items.question: For two portfolio pieces still in development, write one sentence about what you learned from each, then one sentence about the progress you can see between them.
items.hint: Axis: reflection and learning progress. Make the change visible, rather than only saying that there was progress.

items.title: How an overview helps a reader follow the theme
items.question: Write how you would use a short overview so a reader can follow your Form 6 theme: what you would say first, and which work or research page you would use as evidence.
items.hint: Axis: visual expression and structure. The overview is a structure exercise. It has no fixed word count, and it is not an official result.
